Can You Find the Brightest Star in the Night Sky?

Episode 120 of a daily journey through the universe. ✨
We visit Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky at magnitude −1.46: just 8.6 light-years away, about 25 times brighter than the Sun, the Dog Star, why it twinkles in colors, and Sirius B, a white dwarf first seen in 1862.

segments.text: Can you find the brightest star in the night sky? It hides a tiny secret.
After the planets and the Moon, Sirius is the brightest thing in the night sky.
segments.headline: The brightest star

segments.text: It shines at magnitude minus one point four six.
Part of the reason: it's close. Only about eight point six light-years away. One of our nearest neighbors.
It's also about twenty-five times brighter than our Sun.
segments.headline: 25 times the Sun

segments.text: It's called the Dog Star, because it's the brightest star in the constellation Canis Major, the Big Dog.
segments.headline: The Dog Star

segments.text: When it's low in the sky, Sirius twinkles in flashing colors. That's Earth's air bending its light.
segments.headline: Flashing colors

segments.text: And it has a secret. A tiny companion, Sirius B, first spotted in eighteen sixty-two.
segments.headline: A hidden companion

segments.text: Sirius B is a white dwarf. As heavy as the Sun, but squeezed down to about the size of Earth.

To find Sirius, follow the three stars of Orion's Belt down and to the left. Tomorrow, we go to those three stars. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
